title: Incremental Multiple Oracle
claim: Final exploitability depends strongly on learning rate and pure-strategy set size, with larger sets reaching far lower exploitability.
layout: 6 panels in 3x2 grid, per-game log-scale curves, legend right of each
description: A 3x2 grid of line plots, each showing exploitability (y-axis, mostly log scale) against training batches (x-axis, 0 to 2e7) for one continuous-action game: Interval, Circle, Glicksberg–Gross, and three Continuous Colonel Blotto variants (2 players/3 items, 3 players/2 items, 3 players/3 items). Each panel has up to 12 coloured curves with shaded variability bands. Curves correspond to learning-rate and strategy-set-size pairs, listed in a legend to the right of each panel. Small sets (size 1 or 2) stay at high exploitability, while larger sets (8 to 32) fall steeply, in some games by several orders of magnitude. The eye goes first to the steep drops and the spread between curve groups. Colours are the same family across panels.
caption: Exploitabilities of learned mixed strategies (part 1).
abstract: We present a framework for computing approximate mixed-strategy Nash equilibria of continuous-action games. It is a modification of the multiple oracle algorithm, which extends the double oracle algorithm to multiple players and continuous action spaces. Unlike prior oracle-based methods, it maintains fixed-cardinality pure strategy sets for each player. Thus, its memory requirements do not grow with the number of iterations. Furthermore, it does not require exact metagame solving on each iteration, which can be computationally expensive for large metagames. Moreover, it does not require global best-response computation on each iteration, which can be computationally expensive or even intractable for high-dimensional action spaces and general games. Our method gradually reduces the exploitability of the strategy profile in the finite metagame, pushing it toward Nash equilibrium. Simultaneously, it gradually improves the pure strategies against this strategy profile in the full game. We evaluate our method on various continuous-action games, showing that it obtains approximate mixed-strategy Nash equilibria with low exploitability.
